Balthasar Meisner
bal'ta-sar mize'ner
n. (Balthasar Meisner, 1587–1626, Wittenberg theologian, author of the Sober Philosophy)
Akkadian through Hebrew Belteshazzar, the traditional name of one of the eastern magi; German Meisner, of Meissen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Balthasar Meisner taught at Wittenberg and died at thirty-nine, leaving among other works the Philosophia Sobria, an examination of how far philosophy may be used in theology and where it must stop. His answer was that reason is a true instrument in its own sphere, serves well in defining terms and detecting fallacies, and has no authority to decide what God has revealed; where philosophy contradicts Scripture, philosophy is wrong. The dictionary commends that answer and commends the title. Sober is exactly the right word, and the two intemperate alternatives were as common then as now: a theology that lets Aristotle set the agenda, and a piety that refuses to think and calls the refusal faith. Meisner, a confessional Lutheran who differed from the Reformed on the Supper and on election, is on this question a reliable guide, and the dictionary says so without pretending the other differences away.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sober as temperate and not intoxicated, and philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes and reasons.

expand to see more

SO'BER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; not intoxicated; habitually temperate; grave; serious.

PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of phenomena as explained by and resolved into causes and reasons.

REA'SON, n. A faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and good from evil.

FAL'LACY, n. Deceptive or false appearance; sophism; a deceitful argument.

Key Scripture

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

1Co 3:19 — "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness."

1Co 2:13 — "Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual."

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Modern Corruption

His Sober Philosophy made reason an instrument in theology and denied it any authority over revelation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the pair of errors Meisner named. One lets a philosophical system set the terms, so that revelation is admitted only where a prevailing account of reality has room for it — the method of every age's accommodating theology, ours included. The other treats all careful thinking as pride and leaves the Christian unable to define a word or follow an argument, which does not protect doctrine but surrenders it to whoever argues most confidently.

The principle to recover is that revelation rules and reason serves. “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19). The apostolic manner of speaking is taught by the Spirit and not by human wisdom: “not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth” (1Co 2:13). And the test is always the same — “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

Usage

"“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) — the Sober Philosophy of 1611."

"“the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19) — reason as instrument, not as judge."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — a title that is itself the argument."
